label: copy-phase input 3 (fed-back digit 3)
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase, only when the fed-back input token is the digit 3 (never on any other token, never in the original phase or at <DEL>). Recall is 100%; ~25% of copy-phase 3 inputs stay inactive (mostly low-magnitude borderline cases). Strongest when the 3 is fed back early in the copy (recall_idx 2-3, e.g. sequences starting X 3 3 ...), and within runs of consecutive 3s the first is largest and later ones decay. Never fires on 3 in the original phase.

issues: Core claims hold. Activation is zero in the original phase and at <DEL>, and zero on every token other than 3 (in_tok=3 has 100% of activation mass, copy phase has 100%). Recall is 1.0 and mass recall is 1.0 on both dev and test. Test scores: P 0.748, R 1.0, F1 0.856.

Calling the false positives 'borderline cases' understates them. They follow position in a graded way: precision is 0.98 at recall_idx 2, 0.90 at 3, 0.80 at 4, 0.63 at >=5 (0.62 when to_go<=1) and 0.55 at recall_idx 1. So the feature is weak or silent on a 3 fed back right after <DEL> (the sequence starts with 3) and on 3s late in the copy. Activation fades with recall position; nothing switches it off cleanly. No position cut beats the base predicate: recall_idx>=2 gives F1 0.832 and 2<=recall_idx<=6 gives 0.814, against 0.859 for the base predicate.

The claim that later 3s in a run decay is only partly supported. In the top examples the first 3 of a run is largest. But a 3 right after another 3 is active slightly MORE often than average (precision 0.79 vs 0.75), so 'decay' describes magnitude, not whether it fires.

I found no other systematic class of false positives. Precision barely moves with n_digits (0.75 for 1 digit, 0.75 for 3 or more), L, in_count, earlier 3s (0.79), a vowel or digit before, a digit after, or correct (0.75). The inactive cases look like the low end of a graded magnitude, not a missing condition.
The label does not overclaim relative to the predicate.
